findings.line_or_range: PUT /calendars (~line 194-210) and GET /calendars selected computation / selectedCalendarIds
findings.concern: PUT /calendars with an empty calendarIds array deletes all rows from google_calendar_selections but inserts none (guarded by `if (ids.length > 0)`), leaving the table with zero rows. GET /calendars and selectedCalendarIds() both treat zero rows as 'never chosen' and silently resolve back to primary-only, so an owner who explicitly deselects every calendar has that choice silently overwritten on the very next read. This directly contradicts the schema's own documented invariant in src/worker/db/schema.ts ('the schema cannot express that difference, so the route owns it explicitly') — the route does not, in fact, own it explicitly for the zero-selection case.

findings.line_or_range: it("issues no non-GET request to the Calendar API") ~line 67-83
findings.concern: The per-call AC-13 guard is still constructible-defeatable after three prior fix rounds: (1) it only matches literal call tokens `fetch(`/`fetchImpl(`, so a call reached through `new Request(url,{method:'POST'})` then `fetch(request)`, or through a renamed/aliased fetch import, or through a wrapping helper function, is invisible to it; (2) it only matches a literal quoted method string via `method:\s*["'](?:POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE)["']`, so `method: someVariable` evades it entirely; (3) the 500-character window is anchored at the fetch/fetchImpl call token itself, so a URL or method assembled more than ~500 characters into that same call's init object falls outside the window and is missed. This is the sole automated enforcement of the ADR-0007 read-only consent boundary (AC-13), so a guard with multiple known-constructible bypasses is a false sense of security on a compliance-critical invariant, not a cosmetic gap.

On a non-2xx response with an unparseable JSON body, `payload` stays `{}` and `payload.error === "invalid_grant"` is false, so the function reports `http_400` (etc.) instead of `invalid_grant` even when the real cause is a dead/revoked credential. This misroutes /calendars and /events to a 502 'try again later' instead of the 'reconnect your calendar' distinction the function's own doc comment says exists specifically to avoid this collapse. Google's OAuth error bodies are documented as always JSON so likelihood is low, but the failure is silent and self-contradicting against the function's stated purpose.

Individual malformed/unmappable events are silently dropped (toCalendarEventDto returning null) with no count or flag returned, unlike calendar-level failures which are named via failedCalendars. The plan explicitly accepts null-on-malformed-row as the mitigation but does not require reporting a count, so this is advisory only, not a plan violation.

"PROSPECTIVE hardening against the evasions review named" cites no existing test:line whose assertion currently contradicts a PRD AC - it requests advance clearance for an edit that has not been made. Step 3.2 of this agent's contract requires a disputed_tests citation to name a real, already-present test assertion the dispute contests; there is none to arbitrate here, so DISPUTE_REJECTED on procedural grounds - not a ruling that the anticipated edit would be wrong. This channel resolves a concrete, already-diffed contradiction between a specific test and a specific PRD AC, as items 1 and 2 were; it does not pre-authorize a future edit to a file the prior standard-mode review's own R-X finding already treated as test-glob-matched. If, after making the change, R-X flags it in the next standard-mode review, raise a fresh TEST_CONTRACT_DISPUTE citing the actual resulting diff:lines against PRD AC-13 - exactly the process items 1 and 2 followed. Substantive answer to the secondary question asked (advisory only, not part of the verdict): a regex/string-matching structural guard over 'every fetch call site in src/' cannot be made SOUND against a determined adversary - new Request() + fetch(request), a renamed or re-exported fetch binding, an indirection through a wrapper function, and a method assembled into a variable are all constructions no regex over source text can universally catch, because they require tracing data and control flow the regex has no model of. The honest fix is not a better regex; it is to NARROW the guard's claim to what pattern matching over source text can actually prove - a literal, unaliased fetch(...) / fetchImpl(...) call site with an inline literal method string, which is the only call shape this codebase's own client.ts uses today - and say so plainly in the docstring, OR replace the mechanism with something that has an actual data-flow model, such as an ast-grep/ts-morph rule that resolves import aliases and follows simple const-bound Request objects, or, more robust than either, a single injected-fetch chokepoint enforced at the type level so there is only ever one call site to audit. Widening the regex window past 500 characters or adding a few more literal evasion patterns repeats the last three rounds' mistake and should not be represented as closing the gap.

Item A (source-invariants.test.ts, docstring+describe-rename only, committed 64b56b5, diffed 64b56b5~1..64b56b5). Verified by diff: the only non-comment change is the describe() title string ("AC-13 — read-only by construction" -> "AC-13 tripwire — no ACCIDENTAL write reaches the Calendar API"); every it() body, every expect(), the CODE construction, and the regex-based detection logic are byte-identical to the version already cleared at attempt 2 item 2. So: is this a D17 test modification, or documentation living inside a test file? Both, and that is exactly why it is REJECTED rather than exempted. D17's own mechanism (this jsonl, attempt 2 item 4: "R-X's canonical pathspec set ... is matched at the FILE level by git diff --name-only -- <pathspec> - any diff touching this file, addition or edit, will appear in that list") is deliberately content-blind — it does not parse whether a diff touches an assertion, a comment, or a string literal, precisely so that no edit to a test-glob file gets to argue its own harmlessness unreviewed. So mechanically this file remains R-X-caught, full stop, regardless of the answer to the philosophical half of the question. But Step 3.3 of this channel asks a narrower thing than R-X asks: does the CITED TEST's expected behavior contradict the CITED AC's plain reading? Here it cannot, because nothing about what the test expects changed — the assertions were already independently validated as correct and sound against PRD AC-13 (PRPs/prds/google-calendar-read.prd.md:75) at attempt 2 item 2, and this edit does not touch them. There is therefore no test-vs-PRD contradiction for this channel to arbitrate and uphold; the dispute's implicit claim that an exception is warranted here does not hold up, because 'the edit is harmless' and 'the edit corrects a contradiction between a test and the PRD' are different claims, and only the second is what DISPUTE_UPHELD_TEST_WRONG or DISPUTE_UPHELD_PRD_AMBIGUOUS can recognize. DISPUTE_REJECTED. Consistency note, since the disputer explicitly asked for consistency over leniency: this is not a ruling that comment-only edits are dangerous, or that this specific edit is unwelcome — the content is accurate and, per attempt 2 item 3's own advisory, the honest direction to take the docstring in. It is a ruling that this dispute channel's three outcomes are built around assertion-vs-AC contradictions, this edit contains none, and R-X's file-level, content-blind design (a deliberate choice, not an oversight, per D17's 'no grace period' text) supplies no separate carve-out for edits it cannot distinguish from a substantive one. The practical consequence for the pipeline, stated plainly since it is real: as things stand, a docstring-only edit to a test-glob file has no path to a cleared R-X row through this channel, because the channel has nothing to uphold in its absence of a contradiction — the only way to keep R-X green on this file is to not include a diff against it in the reviewed range at all. That is worth raising to the owner as a modeling gap in the arbitration outcome taxonomy (a fourth outcome along the lines of DISPUTE_MOOT_NO_CONTRADICTION would resolve it more honestly than forcing this into REJECTED), not something this ruling can fix by stretching REJECTED's or UPHELD's definitions to fit.

None of the three ACs is ambiguous; none of the new assertions asks for a strained or alternate reading. Each addition directly evidences a defect this same reviewer's own R-SEM findings had already identified as high-severity (attempt 1, PUT /calendars empty-array silent-loss finding; attempt 3, DELETE /connection AC-4 finding) or explicitly required (attempt 1's accessTokenFor invalid_grant finding). Category fit, stated plainly rather than glossed over: DISPUTE_UPHELD_TEST_WRONG's own text ('the cited test's expected behavior contradicts the cited AC's plain reading') presumes an EXISTING test being corrected; these are net-new tests, so there was no prior 'wrong' assertion to fix, only a coverage gap. That is a genuine mismatch between this case and the category's literal wording, not a technicality being overlooked. UPHELD_TEST_WRONG is used here as the closest available fit, on the same basis this reviewer's attempt-2 item-4 ruling already forecast ('these additions ... are the more straightforward case: they are new coverage of the plan's own AC-A7/AC-A8 and the committed R-SEM fixes, not a change to an existing assertion's meaning') and because the alternative outcomes fit even worse: PRD_AMBIGUOUS is plainly false (none of the three ACs is ambiguous), and REJECTED would mean asserting that AC-15/AC-4/AC-11 do NOT support what these tests expect, which is false on the text. Direct answer to the meta-question asked, since it is the one that matters most for the pipeline: yes, under the current design, adding a test that is the only available evidence for a reviewer's own finding costs a mandatory arbitration round EVERY time, with no exception for purely-additive, uncontested, PRD-grounded content. R-X's file-level, content-blind match (D17, 'no grace period') does not distinguish a new assertion proving compliance from an edit weakening one; that is deliberate, to close exactly the loophole D17 exists to close, but it has the acknowledged side effect priced into this ruling: every review round whose R-SEM half finds a behavioral gap best evidenced by new test content, rather than existing content, generates a second, mandatory arbitration round before the fix can be marked APPROVED, even when — as in items 1, 2 and this one — the outcome is not seriously in doubt. That is a real, recorded pipeline cost, not a hypothetical one, and the schema's three-outcome menu has no dedicated category for 'new, uncontested, PRD-grounded coverage' distinct from 'an existing test was wrong' — both items A and B in this ruling surface the same underlying gap in the outcome taxonomy from two different directions (A: nothing to uphold because nothing contradicts; B: something to uphold but the wrong-shaped category). Recommending a fourth outcome (e.g. DISPUTE_UPHELD_NEW_COVERAGE) to the pipeline layer, not silently stretching the existing three to cover it forever.
